title: Trial procedure: Advance disclosure protects courtroom management
desc: Moves technology disputes outside the jury’s hearing while preserving evidence rules, presentation distinctions and procedural relief.

kps.k: The supplied material concerns trial management, not the merits of AI-use certification.
kps.d: Despite their AI-certification labels, both summaries describe Judge Brantley Starr’s courtroom procedures. They provide no substantive basis to assess the Fifth Circuit’s proposed certification rule, public disagreement over it, or its June 2024 non-adoption. The supported theme is advance preparation and judicial control of evidence and courtroom time. These are procedural requirements and stated rationales, not empirical evidence of effectiveness or competing positions on AI regulation.

kps.k: Advance disclosure moves disputes outside the jury’s hearing without replacing formal evidentiary safeguards.
kps.d: Starr requires counsel to disclose the next day’s witnesses and exhibits at 6pm and explain maintained objections by 8pm, enabling argument before the jury arrives. Similar deadlines govern opening and closing demonstratives. Preliminary rulings do not admit exhibits: counsel must still offer them before the jury with a witness on the stand. The guidance also distinguishes authentication of email headers from the separate evidentiary requirements for email contents. In practice, counsel must prepare both timely disclosures and an adequate foundation.

qs.q: - Counsel presenting testimony must disclose by email to opposing counsel and court staff at 6pm each evening the witnesses and exhibits it plans to introduce the following day.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: - By 8pm, opposing counsel must respond with which pretrial written objections it maintains in explanatory form, not shorthand form.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: The procedures distinguish presentation aids from evidence the jury may consider during deliberations.
kps.d: Trial-created demonstratives ordinarily receive identification markings only; counsel may display them, but they do not accompany the deliberating jury. Starr excepts charts or summaries necessary to understand the evidence. Advance review also requires counsel to revise opening and closing demonstratives when the court sustains objections. The distinction limits what presentation materials can become part of the jury’s evidentiary record; the excerpts do not address AI-generated materials specifically.

qs.q: Charts or Summaries in Evidence:  Generally speaking, the Court treats documents created for trial as demonstratives that get marked as exhibits for identification only.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Such documents are not evidence and do not go back to the jury, but they may be published to the jury during trial.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Time budgets and controls on objections encourage efficient presentation while preserving specified routes for relief.
kps.d: Starr allocates hours per party in civil and some criminal trials, counting jury-facing time and unsuccessful sidebars against that allocation. He considers prior efficiency when deciding requests for additional time. The court prohibits speaking objections before jurors and disfavors interruptions during opening and closing, but permits subsequent requests for relief and intervenes when an opening violates a limine ruling. Advance deposition rulings, agreed arrangements for shared witnesses and preapproved voir dire questions further reduce in-court disputes. These measures express the court’s efficiency rationale rather than demonstrate measured time savings.

qs.q: - Time that counts against a party’s limit is time spent in front of the jury or time spent at a sidebar that the party loses.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: In determining whether to grant more time, the Court will consider whether a requesting party has efficiently used its previous time.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The settlement guidance makes timing consequential for confidentiality.
kps.d: Starr encourages settlement at least two weeks before trial. The guidance states that parties retain a right to confidential settlement agreements only before the jury is sworn and must disclose settlements reached during trial through an unredacted filing or in open court to moot the case and discharge the jury. Counsel therefore need to account for this stated courtroom requirement when advising on settlement timing; the material supplies no broader legal debate over the requirement.

qs.q: - Settlements During Trial:  Parties should strive to settle at least two weeks before trial.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: The parties only have a right to confidential settlement agreements before a jury is sworn in.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-bodies material supports the proposition as a statement of Judge Starr’s trial-management approach. Across the paired records, the common rationale is to move evidentiary disputes and legal argument outside the jury’s hearing through advance disclosure and morning review, reducing disruption and sidebar time while retaining ordinary evidentiary safeguards. In particular, advance rulings do not themselves admit exhibits; foundation, authentication and formal admission remain necessary. The procedures also reinforce the proposition through controls on demonstratives, objections, trial-time allocation, voir dire and settlement disclosure. Internal variation is limited: the second record adds detail on deposition designations and written rulings, while the first includes additional matters such as post-verdict custody. Neither record provides empirical evidence that the procedures improve efficiency, and neither substantively addresses AI-use certification despite the source labels. Accordingly, this evidence should not be generalized to regulators, courts or professional bodies more broadly, nor treated as a position on AI regulation.

qs.q: If it doesn’t, the Court handles exhibit objections on the record but outside the hearing of the jury to the extent possible.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: - If the Court overrules all objections to an exhibit at the pretrial conference or in the morning session, it does not mean that exhibit is admitted into evidence.
qs.a: Mandatory Certification Regarding Generative Artificial Intelligence (Judge Brantley Starr, N.D. Tex., standing order) · Regulators & courts · 2023

elens.an: The supplied 2023–2024 sources support the cluster proposition that advance disclosure and judicial review move evidentiary and other legal disputes outside the jury’s hearing while preserving formal safeguards. Both describe evening disclosure and objection deadlines followed by pre-jury review; both also distinguish preliminary objection rulings from the later formal admission of evidence. Their shared rationale is courtroom efficiency—especially reducing sidebars and legal argument before jurors—without relaxing foundation, authentication, hearsay or admission requirements. Material internal variation is limited: one record gives broader attention to time extensions, settlement and post-verdict custody, while the other adds deposition-designation and voir dire procedures. These differences extend the procedural detail but do not create disagreement. Importantly, despite the sources’ AI-related labels and placement in the “Generative shock” period, the supplied excerpts do not substantively address AI-use certification or evaluate AI policy; they support only the trial-management proposition. The two records also substantially duplicate the same procedural material, so they should not be treated as independent evidence of prevalence or wider judicial consensus.
